name: record-set
intent: Carry a query result between layers as a single in-memory tabular value - rows plus the column metadata that describes them - so consumers can iterate, filter and reshape the data without holding a database cursor or depending on the producing layer's types.
problem: A result set is needed away from the code that produced it (a Table Module, a reporting view, a UI grid, a batch step, a test), but a live cursor cannot travel: database cursors are connection-bound, non-serialisable and die when the producing call returns. Wrapping each result in its own purpose-built class invents one type per query shape, and handing back entities pulls domain types across the boundary.
context: Data-oriented enterprise applications where several components consume the same tabular projection: a Table Module applying set-oriented logic to a whole table, a reporting or export path, a UI grid, an offline client, or tests that need canned results. Applies where the projection is query-defined and consumers want generic row/column access; less relevant when a typed collection of domain objects can travel instead.
benefits: One uniform container covers every projection: no per-query wrapper classes, and no entity or ORM types crossing the boundary.
Detachment: the set outlives the cursor and connection that produced it, so consumers may iterate, cache, serialise or ship it to another tier without holding database resources.
Generic consumers work against columns they never saw at compile time - grids, exporters, report writers, admin tools and tests.
The data shape is decoupled from both the database schema and the domain model, so schema changes and refactorings do not ripple through consumers.
Cheap and uniform to construct from any source (SQL result, CSV, in-memory computation, test fixture), which makes the producer substitutable.
tradeoffs: Column access is weakly typed: names and indices resolve at runtime, so typos and schema drift become production errors unless a typed wrapper is layered on top.
Whole-result materialisation: the set is loaded into memory, so unbounded queries need paging or streaming (Cursor Pagination) rather than 'just fetch it all'.
Snapshot semantics: the value is stale as soon as it is built and carries no optimistic-lock signal; updating through it needs identity and version columns, or a Unit of Work.
Metadata drift: the header travels with the data but the container cannot enforce it, so producer and consumer can silently disagree about types, nullability or units.
Temptation to give the container behaviour (validation, computed columns, change tracking such as DataRow states) pulls domain logic back into what was meant to be a neutral value.
Over-fetching: a generic tabular payload exposes every selected column to every consumer, which leaks fields and couples clients to incidental columns.

participants.responsibility: The detached tabular value itself: an ordered collection of rows plus the shared column metadata (names, order, and - where the producer knows them - types and nullability).
One tuple of column values, addressable by position or by column name; a value with no identity and no persistence behaviour.
The descriptor that travels with the rows and makes generic access possible: column names, order, and type/format information.
Builds the set from a query, file or computation and hands it over already detached from the data source (cursor closed, connection released).
Works on the set as a whole - iterate, filter, project, bind to a grid, export, assert - without a connection and without domain-model types.

use_cases: Reporting and export endpoints that render arbitrary query projections (CSV, spreadsheet, PDF, print view) without one class per report.
Table Module business logic operating set-wise over a whole table, where the Table Data Gateway hands back a record set and the module passes it on.
A boundary endpoint returning a tabular payload (rows plus column headers) that a client grid or spreadsheet binds directly.
Test fixtures: a canned in-memory record set stands in for a database query so service and UI tests run without a database.
Ad-hoc administration and BI-style screens where the user composes the projection at runtime and the column set is genuinely data.
Batch/ETL steps that pass a tabular chunk downstream after the source cursor has been closed.
.NET ADO.NET DataTable/DataSet materialises relational rows locally while retaining DataColumn schema and DataRow values for disconnected reporting, table-module, or export work.
A pandas DataFrame carries labeled row and column axes for heterogeneous tabular data, making a detached projection easy to filter, reshape, and export from CSV or query adapters.
An Apache Arrow Table packages equal-length chunked columns with an explicit schema and can be assembled from or streamed as record batches for columnar interchange.
avoid_when: The result has a fixed, known shape and travels between compiled layers: a typed collection (List<Order>) or a Data Transfer Object is safer and self-documenting.
The consumer will map the rows into domain objects anyway: fetch straight into those objects (Active Record, Data Mapper, Row Data Gateway) and skip the intermediate tabular value.
The result is large or unbounded: stream rows from the cursor (sqlite3_step, sql.Rows.Next, Sequel#stream, fetchmany) or page with Cursor Pagination instead of materialising everything.
The payload is a stable remote contract: a Data Transfer Object documents the wire shape, while a generic record set leaves the contract implicit and version-fragile.
The data is a single entity with behaviour: a record set pushes field-name strings and null-handling into callers where a domain object would carry them.
anti_patterns: Returning a generic record set from every repository method so callers must know column names as strings - an untyped schema smeared across the codebase.
Using DataTable/ResultSet as the application's domain model and editing rows in place, so business rules end up in UI code or in the container's events.
Passing a live, connection-bound cursor (ResultSet, sql.Rows) as if it were a detached value, so consumers see closed cursors or hold connections open.
Materialising every query result 'in case the caller needs it', producing memory blow-ups and over-fetching of sensitive columns.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: data shapes and data access are distinct from domain behaviour - a record set carries values, not rules.
Uniformity over specialisation: one generic tabular container beats a class per query shape - when the shape is genuinely dynamic.
Loose coupling across boundaries: consumers depend on a neutral tabular value, not on the producer's entities or on a live cursor.
Explicit schema: metadata travels with the data so consumers can validate instead of assume.
Honest typing: where the shape is known, typed views (DTOs, typed containers, mapped records) belong on top of the generic container.
best_practices: Ship the column header with the rows and route column access through it; never rely on positional order alone.
Keep the record set a pure value: no connection, no cursor, no persistence methods, no behaviour beyond row/column access.
Layer typed access on top (typed DataSet, mapped record, DTO projection) as soon as the shape is stable.
Bound the set: page, limit or stream, and select only the columns the consumer actually needs.
Freeze or copy the set before handing it over so consumers cannot mutate shared state.
Never hand a live cursor across a layer boundary; materialise into the detached form first.
sources: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2003) - Record Set (Base Patterns, Chapter 18): "An in-memory representation of tabular data".
